alt: A transverse wave with crests and troughs whose points oscillate up and down, at right angles to the direction of travel. A longitudinal wave on a slinky with compressions (C) and rarefactions (R) whose coils oscillate backwards and forwards, along the direction of travel.
caption: Compare the direction of oscillation with the direction the wave travels.

alt: A transverse wave: wavelength is from one crest to the next; amplitude is from the rest position to a crest, while crest to trough is twice the amplitude. For a longitudinal wave the wavelength is from the centre of one compression to the centre of the next. Wavefronts seen from above are lines along the crests, one wavelength apart.
caption: Amplitude is measured from the rest position; wavelength is a distance along the wave.

alt: Three snapshots of ripples moving to the right past a floating cork. The wave shape moves on, but the cork stays on the same vertical line and only bobs up and down. Waves transfer energy and information; the water and air particles oscillate about fixed positions.
caption: The wave moves on; the cork, like the water, just bobs about one place.

alt: v = f × λ and f = 1 / T, since a wave moves one wavelength in one period. In a ripple tank, 12 waves in 4.0 s gives f = 3.0 Hz; 5 wavelengths across 7.5 cm gives λ = 0.015 m; so v = 0.045 m/s and T = 0.33 s. A 256 Hz tuning fork in air at 340 m/s gives λ = 1.33 m.
caption: Find f and λ from what you measure, convert to m, then v = f × λ.

alt: Left: plane water waves hit a wall and are reflected back. Right: water waves cross from deep to shallow water at an angle; in shallow water they are slower, the wavefronts are closer together and they change direction towards the normal. Worked example: at 5.0 Hz, 0.30 m/s gives λ = 0.060 m and 0.20 m/s gives λ = 0.040 m.
caption: In refraction speed and wavelength change; frequency stays the same.

alt: A source moving to the right emits circular wavefronts, each centred where the source was when it was emitted. Ahead, observer A receives squashed wavefronts: shorter wavelength, higher frequency. Behind, observer B receives spread-out wavefronts: longer wavelength, lower frequency. The source frequency itself does not change.
caption: Bunched wavefronts ahead mean shorter wavelength and higher observed frequency.
